title: Audit Logging Overview (One-Pager)
author: Kevin Osei
content:
## Purpose
This one-pager describes Redwood Inference’s audit logging capabilities for enterprise security reviews: (1) what we log, (2) how events are structured, (3) export/integration options, and (4) differences across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Audit logs are intended to support customer governance, change tracking, and investigations related to administrative and security-relevant activity.

**Last reviewed:** 2026-02-06  
**Owner:** Security (Audit Logging)  
**Customer-facing use:** Yes (safe to share)

---

## What audit logs are (and are not)
**Audit logs capture control-plane activity** and security-relevant events associated with Redwood accounts/organizations, users, roles, credentials, and configuration.

Audit logs are **not** designed to be a full content log of inference payloads. By default, audit logs do not include full prompt/response contents. Where request identifiers or metadata are logged for correlation, they are limited to operationally necessary fields.

If a customer requires additional application-level logging (e.g., request/response capture for their own compliance needs), Redwood recommends implementing that in the customer application layer and/or using Redwood’s supported telemetry hooks where applicable.

---

## Event categories (high level)
Redwood audit logs are organized into categories to simplify filtering and SIEM routing.

### 1) Identity & Access Management (IAM)
Events that reflect changes to who can access Redwood and what they can do.
- User invited/activated/deactivated
- Role granted/revoked
- Permission or policy changes (where applicable)
- Service account created/rotated (if enabled for the tenant)

### 2) Authentication & SSO Configuration
Events that reflect authentication posture.
- SSO/SAML enabled/disabled
- SSO certificate/metadata updated
- SCIM provisioning changes (if enabled)
- MFA/admin session settings changes (where supported)

### 3) Credential & Key Management
Events related to credentials used to call the API.
- API key created, updated (e.g., label/scope), revoked
- Key rotation events (when performed through Redwood Console/API)
- Token issuance/validation failures may be surfaced as security events (rate-limited)

### 4) Organization, Project, and Workspace Administration
Events that impact tenant structure and ownership.
- Organization/project created/archived
- Billing/admin ownership changes (administrative)
- Workspace settings changes

### 5) Model & Serving Configuration (Control Plane)
Events that reflect changes to runtime configuration initiated through the control plane.
- Model enabled/disabled for a project
- Deployment configuration changes (e.g., routing policy updates, fallback policy changes)
- Rate limit/quota policy updates
- Endpoint configuration changes

### 6) Data Governance & Logging Settings
Events related to retention, exports, and audit log delivery configuration.
- Audit log export target created/updated/removed
- Retention configuration updated (where configurable)
- Data deletion request submitted/processed (status events; see retention one-pager for specifics)

### 7) Security & Administrative Actions
Events that may indicate security-relevant activity.
- Admin privilege escalation actions (e.g., role change to elevated role)
- Repeated auth failures (summarized)
- Support access enablement/disablement (where applicable and configured)

**Note:** Exact event availability can vary by deployment mode and enabled features. If a customer has a specific questionnaire item (e.g., “log all admin actions including X”), route to Security/GRC for confirmation against current capabilities.

---

## Common event types (examples)
Below are representative examples. Actual event type strings may differ slightly by UI label/version.

| Category | Example event type | Typical description |
|---|---|---|
| IAM | user.invited | Admin invited a new user to the organization |
| IAM | user.deactivated | User access disabled |
| IAM | role.granted | Role assigned to a user or group |
| Auth/SSO | sso.enabled | SSO turned on |
| Auth/SSO | sso.metadata.updated | SAML metadata/cert updated |
| Credentials | api_key.created | New API key created |
| Credentials | api_key.revoked | API key revoked |
| Org/Admin | project.created | New project created |
| Model/Serving | model.enabled | Model made available for a project |
| Model/Serving | routing.policy.updated | Routing/fallback policy updated |
| Governance | audit_export.created | SIEM/export integration created |
| Governance | audit_export.updated | Export destination or filters updated |

---

## Log schema (fields customers can expect)
Audit events are emitted as structured records. The exact field set can vary slightly by category/event type, but typical fields include:

- **timestamp**: Event time (UTC)
- **event_type**: Normalized event name (e.g., `api_key.revoked`)
- **event_category**: High-level category (e.g., `credentials`)
- **severity**: Informational / warning / security (when applicable)
- **actor**: Who performed the action (user ID/service account ID); may include email/username depending on tenant configuration
- **actor_type**: user / service_account / system
- **target**: What was affected (e.g., api_key ID, user ID, org/project ID)
- **request_context**: IP address (when available), user agent (when available), request ID / correlation ID
- **outcome**: success / failure (when applicable)
- **metadata**: Additional key/value details relevant to the event (e.g., role name, policy identifier)

### Redaction and minimization
To reduce sensitivity, audit logs are designed to avoid embedding customer prompt/response payloads. Where identifiers are included for correlation, they are limited and intended to support incident response and operational tracing.

---

## Export and SIEM integration options
Export options depend on deployment mode. In general, customers can:

1) **View and search in Redwood Console**
- Filter by time range, category, actor, and event type
- Download results (format availability may vary)

2) **Programmatic access (API)**
- Retrieve audit events for ingestion into customer systems
- Supports pagination and time-based filters

3) **Automated delivery (SIEM forwarding)**
When enabled for the tenant/deployment, customers can configure automated delivery to a supported destination.

### Typical integration patterns
- **Pull model (API polling):** Customer SIEM/ETL jobs pull audit events on a schedule.
- **Push model (delivery integration):** Redwood delivers events to a customer-controlled endpoint or log destination, based on configured filters.

### Operational notes
- Delivery/export availability and formats are influenced by the customer’s plan and deployment mode.
- Customers should validate ingestion rate/retention requirements with their SIEM team; Redwood can help size expected event volumes based on enabled features.

---

## Deployment mode differences (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
The table below summarizes how audit logging works across Redwood’s deployment options.

| Topic | Hosted API | Dedicated | Private (VPC / On-Prem) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control plane | Managed by Redwood | Managed by Redwood (isolated capacity) | Customer environment + Redwood-managed control plane components as scoped in the Private architecture |
| Audit log availability | Included for tenant/org admin + security-relevant actions | Included; similar events + dedicated-specific configuration events | Available; event scope depends on which components run in customer environment and configured log sinks |
| Export options | Console + API; automated delivery available for eligible enterprise plans | Console + API; automated delivery commonly enabled for enterprise | Customer-controlled log pipeline; Redwood can integrate with customer SIEM/log stack depending on architecture |
| Data location | Events stored/processed in Redwood-managed cloud regions (see data residency one-pager) | Same as Hosted; may support region pinning per contract | Primarily within customer-controlled environment for customer-hosted components; Redwood components follow Private deployment scope |
| Shared responsibility | Redwood operates audit logging service; customer configures access + exports | Same as Hosted | Customer operates/monitors customer-side log infrastructure; Redwood supports integration and provides component-level events per scope |

**Important:** Private deployments can vary (VPC vs on-prem; customer-managed vs Redwood-managed components). For a regulated customer request (“all logs must remain in our network”), route to Solutions Engineering + Security to confirm the exact Private architecture and logging boundaries.

---

## Access controls and auditability
- Audit logs are accessible to authorized administrative roles following least-privilege principles.
- Administrative actions that change access configuration (e.g., role grants, SSO changes, API key lifecycle) are designed to be auditable.
- Customers can combine audit logs with SSO provider logs (Okta/Azure AD) for end-to-end traceability.

For role definitions and least-privilege guidance, see:
- **SSO/SAML and SCIM (One-Pager)**
- **RBAC Model Reference**

---

## Retention and deletion
Audit log retention depends on plan and deployment mode. Redwood provides a separate customer-facing one-pager for retention defaults and controls.

See: **Data Retention Controls (One-Pager)**.

---

## Validation, compliance, and evidence
- Redwood maintains a security and compliance program and can provide compliance evidence (e.g., SOC 2 Type II report) under NDA via the standard evidence sharing process.
- Audit logging is one of the controls commonly evaluated in security reviews; this document describes product behavior and is not, by itself, a compliance report.

---

## FAQs (common security questionnaire prompts)
**Q: Do you log all administrative actions?**  
A: Redwood audit logs are designed to capture security-relevant and administrative actions within the control plane (e.g., user/role changes, SSO config changes, key lifecycle, export/retention setting changes). Event coverage varies by feature and deployment mode; Redwood can confirm specific event types upon request.

**Q: Can we export audit logs to our SIEM?**  
A: Yes. Customers can export via the Audit Logs API and, for eligible enterprise plans/deployments, configure automated delivery to a customer-controlled destination.

**Q: Are prompts/responses included in audit logs?**  
A: Audit logs are control-plane focused and are designed to avoid including full prompt/response contents by default. Customers requiring payload capture should implement application-layer logging and discuss options with Redwood.

---

## Support and contacts
For security reviews and questionnaires, contact your Redwood account team or email **security@redwoodinference.com**.

If you need a sample event set for SIEM testing, request: **“Audit log sample export (current schema)”** and include the target deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and preferred delivery method.
